Title: Boulder City Council Study Session - July 27, 2023
Overview: The study session covered two items: an update on the police oversight ordinance revision process led by consultant Farah Muscadin, where council discussed ordinance drafting, panel scope, monitor roles, selection criteria, training, and outside counsel, with no formal votes taken. The second item presented Module 3 of the Use Table and Standards update focused on neighborhood centers, including proposals for restaurants, duplexes and townhomes, vehicle-related uses, and other use changes, with council providing direction ahead of a planned October ordinance first reading and November second reading. The meeting ended about 30 minutes early with no formal decisions.

Topic1.Title: Police Oversight Ordinance Revision Update
Topic1.Summary: City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde introduced consultant Farah Muscadin, former Austin oversight director, who presented preliminary observations and a timeline for revising the police oversight ordinance. Her recommendations included removing the independent monitor from the panel as a non-voting member, formalizing onboarding and training within 90 days, and using standard operating procedures for details better suited than ordinance text. Council members asked about ordinance drafting versus implementation, the term oversight, the panel's size, and monitor hiring. Council discussed the ambiguous perceived bias criterion and how the panel's discipline recommendation process should work.

Topic2.Title: Council Comments on Police Oversight and Outside Counsel
Topic2.Summary: Council members thanked Farah and the working group and asked for further attention to training development, a grievance process for disagreements over discipline, and a regular cadence for revisiting the ordinance. Questions about outside counsel led staff to explain that the City Attorney's Office represents all boards and commissions and would hire outside counsel only for significant conflicts. Council asked for a survey of how other cities structure their panels.

Topic3.Title: Use Table Module 3 Neighborhood Centers Overview
Topic3.Summary: Planner Lisa Hood presented the third and final use table module, focused on neighborhood centers in business, downtown, and mixed-use zones, to implement Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan policies on walkable 15-minute neighborhoods. Residential zoning changes were deferred to the future comprehensive plan update. Staff summarized community engagement through a story map, questionnaire (about 190 responses by early July, closing July 31), pop-ups, and working group input. Public input favored more restaurants, small grocery stores, and local retail while expressing concern about auto-oriented uses.

Topic4.Title: Restaurant Approval Streamlining
Topic4.Summary: Staff explained that 12 different restaurant regulations across zones make most restaurants require use review, and proposed raising by-right size thresholds, easing patio size limits, and allowing by-right restaurants in downtown zones. Council members broadly supported simplifying approvals and making Boulder a top place to open a restaurant, with suggestions to extend changes to the Hill and to consider limits on chain restaurants. Staff said the City Attorney would investigate chain restaurant distinctions. Staff noted that revenue is cost recovery and that administrative oversight would remain.

Topic5.Title: Duplexes and Townhomes in Neighborhood Centers
Topic5.Summary: Staff proposed allowing duplexes and townhomes on ground floors by right in BT and BR zones, which currently require use review, while keeping BC retail cores unchanged. Council members were divided: some supported middle housing and transition to residential areas, while others worried about displacing retail, density compatibility, and equity and mixed-income concerns. Staff said it had enough direction to move forward and that the questionnaire would provide additional input.

Topic6.Title: Vehicle-Related Uses in Downtown Zones
Topic6.Summary: Staff proposed prohibiting car washes, drive-throughs, fuel service stations, and fuel sales in downtown zoning districts to support walkability, noting few such uses currently exist downtown and that proposals would still need use review criteria. Council members raised concerns about accessibility for people with mobility limits, pharmacy and food drive-throughs, convenience stores serving food deserts, EV charging, and whether prohibition was needed. Many members preferred retaining review rather than outright prohibition.

Topic7.Title: Other Use Table Changes for Neighborhood Centers
Topic7.Summary: Staff presented additional proposed changes to allow government facilities such as post offices, small retail in mixed-use zones, small-scale medical offices and repair services, small theaters or music venues, and temporary events in mixed-use zones, while reviewing museums, lodges, hostels, and animal hospitals more carefully. Council generally supported the changes, especially retail and post offices, though members asked for more information about hostels and lodges and cautioned about noise and compatibility for performance spaces. Members also urged reimagining older neighborhood centers and consideration of small arts spaces.
